metadata.title: It Never Ran
metadata.source_commit_subject: conformance: run the YAML batch at all; widen verify to 8 subsystems
metadata.series_position: episode 13 — the fix that changed nothing, because the code had never run
metadata.note: cli-explainer spine, weekly work report, claude-hai channel. Episode 13, from the last pushed commit on fix/conformance-multidoc-yaml (08b92d3; origin contains it and the branch is in sync). Direct sequel to episode 12, which diagnosed the multi-document YAML failure as 'the defect is in our checker'. FRAMEWORK: DID THE FIX CHANGE ANYTHING / WHAT DOES THE FALLBACK HIDE / WOULD IT PASS IF IT PARSED NOTHING. Hero beat is B05: all THREE mechanisms reproduced in a standalone interpreter — ComposerError on multi-doc, SyntaxError from the mangled one-line script, and the lazy-generator silent pass. The broken line dates to 2026-10-09, which is episode 7's commit. Falsifiability beat is B08: the four lines and all mechanisms reproduce, but the file totals carry a constant ~102 offset against my git-based replay, with the INCREASE matching to within one file.

beats.role_note: COLD OPEN LAW — composer, ask lands answered. Speaks the author's name.
beats.narration_text: I'm Uday Sonawane, and this is my week on Mycroft. Last episode ended with three valid files failing a check, and me saying the defect was in our checker. I fixed the thing I named. It changed nothing — and that was the actual finding.
beats.new_visual_element: Claude composer, the week's ask, answered

shot.show: the Claude composer with the week's ask and its three-line answer

props.command: claude "I switched to safe_load_all and the result is identical. why?"
output: the YAML batch had never executed
a correct fallback hid it for five weeks
and the fix had a second trap in it

beats.role_note: series continuity — the fix that changed nothing, and why that was the clue
beats.narration_text: Here is where it started. Three Kubernetes manifests, perfectly valid, failing the conformance check because they hold several documents and the checker asked for one. Last week I diagnosed that on camera. This week I changed the loader to the multi-document one, re-ran it, and got exactly the same output. Not a better result. The same one. Which can only mean the code I just edited was not the code producing the answer.
beats.new_visual_element: the fix, and the identical output

shot.show: the loader changed, and the result unchanged
shot.visual_intent: Two bordered cards side by side showing the before and after loader calls, the second in terracotta. Beneath, spanning both, a single card reading 'identical output' with a connector rising to each. One line below: the edited code was not the code producing the answer.

beats.role_note: PROOF rubric — three questions, AS A STRUCTURE before the evidence
beats.narration_text: Three questions. One: did the fix change anything — because if it did not, the thing you edited may not be running. Two: what does the fallback hide — a correct fallback behind a broken primary produces right answers for the wrong reason, forever. Three: would this pass if it parsed nothing — ask it of any checker, because the answer is often yes.
beats.new_visual_element: the three questions, as a numbered structure

shot.show: three numbered cards: DID THE FIX CHANGE ANYTHING / WHAT DOES THE FALLBACK HIDE / WOULD IT PASS ON NOTHING
shot.visual_intent: Three bordered cards land in a row, one per narration step. The third lands in terracotta — it is the trap inside the fix itself — and the rest of the reel is scored against all three.

beats.narration_text: The ask was to find out why the output had not moved, and not to touch anything that was not mine.

shot.show: the composer with the instrumentation ask

props.command: claude "instrument the batch runner — prove whether it executes at all, before changing more"
props.segment: The ask · prove it runs first
output: confirm the batch path actually fires

beats.role_note: ACTUAL-CODE LAW — the line that broke it, verbatim from the parent commit
beats.narration_text: This is the line. It builds a shell command containing an inline Python script, and on the way it replaces every newline with a backslash and an n. Those are two characters, not a line break. Python receives the whole program on one line.

props.title: scripts/conformance.mjs @ the parent commit — the line that broke it
props.sparkLine: A line break became two characters

beats.role_note: HERO BEAT — all three mechanisms reproduced standalone
beats.narration_text: I reproduced all of it on its own, with nothing from the repository running. First, the original complaint: the single-document loader on a valid two-document file raises composer error, expected a single document in the stream. Second, the mangled script: Python answers with syntax error, unexpected character after line continuation character. And third, the trap inside the fix — the multi-document loader is lazy, so if you do not wrap it in a list, it parses nothing, raises nothing, and every file passes.
beats.new_visual_element: the three mechanisms, with their real output

shot.show: ComposerError / SyntaxError / silent pass, all reproduced
shot.visual_intent: Three bordered panels stacked, each with its real interpreter output. The first two in soft ink carry their error text; the third, terracotta, shows no error at all and is labelled 'nothing parsed, every file passes'. Citation strip says all three were reproduced standalone.

beats.role_note: QUESTION 2 — why nothing showed for five weeks
beats.narration_text: So why did nobody notice. Because the catch worked. When the batch threw, the code fell back to checking files one at a time, and that fallback is correct — for single-document files, which is almost all of them. Every run produced right answers. The batch was dead and the output never said so. And the line that killed it was mine, from the ninth of October — the commit I made an episode about, the one that introduced batching to make the check fast.
beats.new_visual_element: the fallback path, and the date

shot.show: throw, catch, fallback, correct answer — and the introducing commit
shot.visual_intent: A vertical flow of four bordered steps: batch throws, catch fires, per-file fallback runs, answer is correct. The last is in ink with a tick; the first in terracotta. Beneath, a chip reading 'introduced 2026-10-09 — the episode about making this check fast'.

beats.role_note: the discipline — whose lines were touched, and whose were not
beats.narration_text: One more thing worth naming, because it is the part that does not show up in a diff summary. Four lines changed, and all four were mine, written on the same day. The per-file fallback still calls the single-document loader — it belongs to another contributor, from August, it is correct for what it does, and it was left alone. And the new import went on its own line rather than being merged into somebody else's.
beats.new_visual_element: the four lines, and what was deliberately not touched

shot.show: 4 lines changed, all one author; the fallback left alone
shot.visual_intent: Left: a bordered card reading '4 lines changed — all from 2026-10-09, same author'. Right, in soft ink: three rows with hollow unticked boxes naming what was NOT touched — the fallback's loader, another contributor's August code, the shared import line.

beats.role_note: the recount — mechanism reproduces, file counts carry a constant offset
beats.narration_text: The recount. The four changed lines are exactly four, and blame puts all of them on the ninth of October under one name — that reproduces. All three mechanisms reproduce. The file counts do not, quite. The commit says the checked surface went from one thousand and thirty-nine files to one thousand eight hundred and fifty-three. Replaying the path rules over the committed tree I get one thousand one hundred and forty-two, and one thousand nine hundred and fifty-five — about a hundred and two more at both ends, because the real walker reads the filesystem and I read git. The increase matches to within one file. So the increase is mine and the totals are the commit's.
beats.new_visual_element: what reproduced and what did not

shot.show: 4 lines and 3 mechanisms verified; the totals offset by ~102 with the delta matching
shot.visual_intent: Left: three ticked rows — four lines, one author, one date; three mechanisms reproduced. Right: a terracotta panel comparing 1,039 to 1,853 against my 1,142 to 1,955, with the delta 814 beside 813 and the line 'the increase matches; the baseline does not'.

beats.role_note: the widening, what was left out on purpose, and the limitation recorded
beats.narration_text: And then the point of all of it. Eight contributor subsystems were added to what the check actually walks — the ones that last episode showed it had never opened. Two were left out deliberately, with the reasons written beside them: the subsystem holding that not-a-number file we found last week, because it would fail every run on a defect nobody here can fix, and the archive, which is kept precisely so it stops changing. Local virtual environments are skipped so nobody compiles their own site-packages. And one line at the bottom of the commit: not tested on the Python version C I uses — only the one on this machine.
beats.new_visual_element: the widening, the exclusions, and the recorded limit

shot.show: 8 subsystems added, 2 excluded with reasons, and the untested-version note
shot.visual_intent: A bordered panel listing the eight added subsystems in two columns. Beside it, a soft-ink panel naming the two excluded with their one-line reasons. Beneath both, a terracotta chip reading 'not tested: the Python version CI uses — only 3.10 available here'.

beats.role_note: scaffolded task — the rubric on the viewer's own tooling, with a GOOD/BAD discriminator
beats.narration_text: Your turn. Find a check in your project that has a fast path and a slow fallback. Then break the fast path on purpose and see whether anything tells you. If the output is identical, you have learned something about every green run you have had since it was written.

shot.show: the composer with the handoff prompt and a GOOD/BAD discriminator

props.command: claude "break the fast path of this check deliberately — does anything in the output change?"
props.segment: Your turn · break the fast path
output: GOOD: the run says which path it took
a silent fallback is an untested primary
